title: Gull Duel: Light the Lantern Mast
audienceRationale: A nine-year-old parses animation instantly but stalls on paragraphs, so the opening is now a five-second wordless show with one spoken line and auto read-aloud everywhere. The same child is sharply sensitive to fairness in scorekeeping: v2 let wrong answers push the same progress bar as right ones, which reads to a kid as 'the game can't tell if I'm good.' v3 splits the two on screen — a round rail that always moves forward (you always finish) and a lantern mast that ONLY correctness can light (you know exactly how well you did) — because that honest split is what makes victory feel earned rather than handed over.
openingPromise: Almost no words. Fog hangs over Brightwater Dock; a dark lantern mast with four glass lanterns looms over a padlocked compass rose. Gully the seagull swoops through the fog, snatches the bigger of two demo slices mid-air, and screeches in triumph. Pip speaks ONE line, read aloud: 'Out-eye the gull, Captain — every right pick lights a lantern and burns the fog.' The promise is shown, not read: light all four lanterns, the fog burns away, the compass wakes.
firstThreeSeconds: Fog rolls, the dark lantern mast silhouettes against grey-gold light, Gully's shadow crosses the planks, and two identical crates slide in carrying same-size rectangle wholes — then everything freezes dead still. Zero text on screen except the fraction tags 1/3 and 1/4. Pip's whistle 'TWEET' opens the round; the prompt is spoken aloud automatically.
firstAction: Tap the crate holding the larger coral shaded part. The whole crate is the tap target — huge and forgiving — and the two wholes sit edge-aligned at identical size so the same-whole constraint is enforced by the staging itself, not by instruction text.
interactionDemonstration: Immediately after Pip's one line, the worked demonstration plays as pure pantomime: two same-size wholes appear, the ghost-overlay slides one on top of the other edge-to-edge so the part sizes visibly compare, and Gully dives onto the bigger part with a happy screech. No narration paragraph — the overlay motion IS the teaching. Replayable anytime between rounds from a whistle icon; every replay is logged to node.N3B.replayRequested.
coreInteraction: Four beats, all read aloud, none timed. Beat 1 (N3B-I1): 1/3 vs 1/4 rectangles on aligned crates — tap the crate with the larger shaded part. Beat 2 (N3B-I2): 1/2 vs 1/4 circles, same gesture. During any decision ALL stimuli freeze; Gully hovers overhead as pure theater and will hover forever — commitment is the tap, resolution comes only after it. Beat 3 (N3B-I3): whistle pitch drops — a pre-cut 4-sector circle rises on a pedestal; tapping a sector fills it coral, tapping another sector MOVES the fill (state is always exactly-one-or-zero shaded; the partition lines are untouchable), then stamp the brass plate to commit. Beat 4 (N3B-I4): fog-quiet finale at the lighthouse door — Pip opens the Dockmaster's Rulebook and asks for the deciding rule via talk, type, or phrase tiles. The single on-request ghost-overlay equality check remains available exactly once during the comparison rounds, per the contract's startingSupport.
mathAsPower: Correctness is the only thing that changes the world. Each correct answer lights one lantern on the mast with an audible FWOOM, and a lit lantern burns away one band of fog — the dock literally gets brighter and more colorful because her part-size judgment was right. Gully, who starts skeptical, lands one perch closer to Reina's shoulder per lit lantern. The shaded compass slice she builds in beat 3 physically slots into the dock's painted compass rose, and her spoken rule is what finally lights the lighthouse beacon itself.
stakes: Two stakes a nine-year-old can feel apart: finishing the trial (the round rail always completes — she can never be locked out) versus how bright her dock is when she gets there (only correctness lights lanterns and lifts fog). Out-eyeing Gully is playful reputation; the fog is the real antagonist. Pip states the fairness rule aloud once: 'Slow eyes or fast eyes, a right pick lights the same lantern.' No round ever times out and no answer is ever cut off.
consequences: Committed answers resolve honestly and immediately. Correct: Gully dives to Reina's slice, the lantern FWOOMs alight, one fog band burns off. Wrong: Gully lands on the actually-bigger slice with her told-you-so head tilt, a ghost-flame flickers inside the dark lantern showing which part WAS bigger, the fog stays — and Pip adds one factual line only ('Same-size wholes — fewer equal parts, bigger pieces'). Crucially, the round rail at the bottom still ticks forward, so she sees plainly: I moved on, but I did not earn that light. Rounds are single-attempt; the finale always happens, but its grandeur is scaled strictly by lit lanterns, never by rounds survived.
recovery: After a wrong comparison, the next round opens with the ghost-overlay icon pulsing once — offered, never forced. If timeToFirstValidActionMs trends under ~1500ms alongside an error, Pip's round-open call becomes 'Look FIRST, then strike' (pacing coaching, not answer coaching). The one contract-permitted equality check remains on request. In beat 3, the brass plate stays dim at zero shaded sectors and Pip says 'One sector for one fourth, Captain' — pure state guidance, legal because every tap is a valid state change. The rulebook accepts speech, typing, or tap-together phrase tiles so explanation friction never blocks the finale. A dark lantern is never mocked: its ghost-flame is quiet, informative, and Gully's coo after a miss is sympathetic comedy, not a buzzer.
progression: Five-second wordless fog-and-gull opening; Pip's single spoken promise line
Pantomime worked demonstration with the ghost-overlay (contract startingSupport), replayable via whistle icon
Beat 1 (N3B-I1): 1/3 vs 1/4 rectangles — commit, honest resolution, lantern 1 lights on correct, fog band 1 burns
Beat 2 (N3B-I2): 1/2 vs 1/4 circles — the wider visual gap second, so a stumble is followed by a winnable round; lantern 2, fog band 2
Whistle pitch drop — beat 3 (N3B-I3): shade exactly one sector of the pre-cut circle, stamp the brass plate; lantern 3, fog band 3, the slice slots into the compass rose
Fog-quiet walk to the lighthouse door as the world stills
Beat 4 (N3B-I4): speak/type/tile the deciding rule; the rulebook inks it live and the lighthouse beacon — lantern 4 — ignites the finale
interactionContinuity: Preserves the established grammar: coral-only shading since N1, the N2 ghost-overlay as the self-check tool, commit-then-resolve on every item, and the talk-or-type conch (now backed by phrase tiles). The aligned-crates staging still extends N1's stacked same-size rectangles. What changes is the reward grammar: progress and success now live on two different objects (rail vs. mast) so the child's mental model of 'moving on' vs. 'doing well' stays clean into later nodes.
worldReaction: The world reacts in layers keyed to lanterns, not rounds: at one lantern the crab crowd emerges from the fog waving flags; at two, the bunting colors saturate and the water starts to sparkle; at three, Gully lands on Reina's route marker and preens; at four, the entire cove flips from fog-grey to high-noon cyan. The candlelit workshop across the harbor stays visible and dignified as the unchosen route. A wrong round produces a reaction too — the truthful ghost-flame and Gully's landing on the real answer — so the world always responds, but only rightness makes it bloom.
payoff: A staged, fully animated finale — nothing static. Stage 1: the beacon ignites and sweeps its light across the dock, catching each lit lantern in a chime arpeggio. Stage 2: the compass rose spins up — a roaring golden spin with Gully riding the needle and confetti bursting from the crab crowd if all lanterns are lit; a plucky, still-charming wobble-and-settle at fewer, with Gully hopping on to give the needle an extra shove (the world helps finish, but the difference is visible and honest). Stage 3: the offshore padlock's chain link SNAPS with a physical recoil, Snip-Claw hurls his '1/4 is BIGGER' sign into the sea, and the rulebook page turns to show Reina's rule inked letter-by-letter under 'Harbor Law: Fair Shares' with her name. Stage 4: Pip stamps the captain's badge and the coral ribbon on the board map animates its way to the dock.
replayVariation: On replay the comparison pairs swap sides and swap whole shapes (beat 1 circles, beat 2 rectangles) while keeping the exact contracted fraction pairs; the fog starts already half-lifted and the challenge framing becomes 'light the mast in gold' — lanterns lit on a fully-correct replay burn gold instead of amber. Gully wears racing goggles as the returning-champion nod. perRoundLatencyMs is shown as a 'personal best' stamp only AFTER each commit, so displayed pace can never pressure the decision itself. Replay is engagement-only evidence.
visualDirection: The core visual arc is fog-to-brilliance: open in desaturated grey-gold, end in cyan-sky high noon — the world's color IS the scoreboard. Comparisons always show same-size wholes on identical, edge-aligned crates. Coral remains the exclusive shading color. Fraction tags 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 in bold dockside stencil on hanging tags are nearly the only on-screen text; everything else is icon plus voice. The lantern mast sits screen-right at all times (persistent, glanceable success state); the round rail is a thin rope-and-knot strip along the bottom (persistent, glanceable progress state). The two never share visual language: lanterns glow, knots just tie.
motionDirection: Snappy 0.4s crate slide-ins deliver momentum, then decision windows are motion-frozen except Gully's single slow readable glide. Correct: 0.7s dive with feather puff, lantern FWOOM with a soft bloom, fog band dissolving as drifting particles over 1.2s. Wrong: 0.8s comic landing on the true answer, ghost-flame flicker in the dark lantern. Beat 3 shading is an instant coral fill; moving it is an instant swap. Finale runs 8–10 seconds of continuous choreographed motion (beacon sweep, needle spin, chain snap recoil, ink flowing letter by letter) — the direct fix for the static payoff. Rulebook beat is preceded by 2s of settling stillness.
soundDirection: Fog-muffled harbor ambience that opens up and brightens with each lantern — the mix itself lifts as fog burns. Pip's whistle marks round-opens with distinct pitches for comparisons vs. the compass slice. Woody crate-thump on tap, brass 'chunk' on submit, FWOOM plus warm chime per lantern, soft descending gull coo on a miss (never a buzzer). Finale: beacon hum, chime arpeggio across lit lanterns, needle whirr, chain SNAP, page-turn, crowd cheer. Every prompt is auto read-aloud with a tap-to-repeat ear icon. All audio respects mute; visual state carries all meaning without sound.
engagementPrediction: started=true, completed=true, zero-to-one assistance requests, timeToFirstValidActionMs <10000 (the near-wordless opening should shrink time-to-first-tap versus v2), frustrationScore ≤0.3, itemAccuracy in the contracted 0.6–0.95 band with at most one fast wrong first-round answer, and a stronger replayRequested likelihood than v2 because a dark lantern gives a concrete, self-chosen reason to run it again ('light them all'). Core design bets: (1) frozen stimuli during decisions let speed excitement coexist with genuine part-size inspection; (2) separating the round rail from the lantern mast makes correctness feel consequential without ever gating completion.
falsifyingEvidence: timeToFirstValidActionMs <1500 paired with an incorrect comparison (striking before inspecting); accuracy <0.6 despite correct N2 interaction points; visible dejection or abandonment after a first dark lantern, indicating the honest-scoreboard split reads as punishment rather than fairness; frustrationScore ≥0.6 in the brisk rounds; a finale watched without reaction or skipped, indicating the animated payoff still fails to land; correct fast selections with a rule citing only the numerals 3 and 4; ≥2 assistance requests contradicting the low-friction prediction; no replay despite an unlit lantern, falsifying the 'light them all' pull.
revisionRationale: Substantial revision, same harbor world. PRESERVED: everything the contract locks and everything the play test validated as strong learning — the item sequence and content, no-timeout frozen-stimuli decisions, single-attempt commit-then-resolve, the one replayable demonstration and one on-request equality check, coral shading, the exactly-one-or-zero sector mechanic, talk/type/tiles explanation, and Gully-lands-on-the-truth honest resolution. CHANGED (1) Progress vs. success: the play test's sharpest flaw was that wrong answers advanced visible dock progress, blurring completion with correctness. v3 splits them into two permanent, visually distinct objects — a rope round rail that always advances (completion is never gated) and a lantern mast that only correct answers can light, with each lit lantern burning a band of fog. Correctness now has an unmistakable, cumulative, world-changing signature; wrongness leaves an honest dark lantern with a truthful ghost-flame. CHANGED (2) Reading load: the text-heavy opening became a five-second wordless pantomime plus one spoken line, with auto read-aloud on all prompts and fraction tags as nearly the only on-screen text. CHANGED (3) Payoff: the mostly-static ending became an 8–10 second staged animated finale (beacon sweep, compass spin, chain snap, live inking, confetti) whose grandeur scales with lit lanterns so the ending also reports achievement honestly. CHANGED (4) Anticipation/changing world: fog-to-brilliance gives the whole activity a visible arc the child drives herself. REPLACED: the accuracy-scaled 'spin richness' as the sole success signal — too subtle and back-loaded; the lantern mast surfaces success continuously instead. The theme was kept rather than swapped because the human's uncertainty is about mechanics and consequence-legibility, and holding the theme constant makes this experiment a clean test of the honest-scoreboard mechanic.
